outcome: The converse of Wolstenholme's theorem (also called Jones' conjecture) — that no composite n satisfies the Wolstenholme congruence binom(2n-1, n-1) ≡ 1 (mod n^3) — remains open as of September 2026; no proof, disproof, or new case-settling result for this specific conjecture was found in the window.
summary: The converse asks whether n prime is the only solution to binom(2n-1,n-1) ≡ 1 (mod n^3), i.e., whether the classical Wolstenholme congruence characterizes primes exactly (equivalently, whether any 'Wolstenholme pseudoprime' composite can satisfy it). I checked the two papers the triage pass flagged, plus wider searches, and found no result in the 26 Jan 2024–present window that settles, narrows, or refutes this specific conjecture. (1) 'Extending Wolstenholme's Theorem: A New Perspective' (Yaqubi & Mirzavaziri, Nov 2024, ResearchGate 386148476) and its follow-up 'New results on Wolstenholme's theorem and its applications' (Mathematics and Society, 2025, math-sci.ui.ac.ir/article_29218) both study a different congruence: binom(np-1, p) mod p^k for prime p and varying n, addressing conjectures of Guo and Krattenthaler about that family of binomial coefficients. This is a related generalization of Wolstenholme-type congruences, not the composite-vs-prime converse question stated in the bullet, and I found no statement in secondary descriptions of either paper claiming to narrow the set of composite integers satisfying the classical converse congruence. Per §3.1 this is a related problem, not a case of the stated one, so it does not count as a change. (2) I found and read about arXiv:2604.16507 ('Deep Vision: A Formal Proof of Wolstenholme's Theorem in Lean 4', Linhares, submitted April 2026), which does disclose genuine AI involvement (a 'relational analogy engine' called Deep Vision plus Claude Code used to write Lean tactics/lemmas, verified by the Lean kernel with zero sorries) — but it formalizes the forward theorem (the classical congruence for primes), not the converse, so it is out of scope for this bullet. (3) A September 2026 paper (arXiv:2609.03091, Guedes & Machado) studies a different congruence, binom(2n,n) ≡ 2^n (mod n), connecting it to perfect numbers and Wieferich primes; this is Wolstenholme-adjacent in spirit but a distinct modular condition from the classical converse, so also out of scope. (4) General searches for 'converse of Wolstenholme's theorem' proof/disproof/new-family results in 2024-2026 turned up nothing beyond restatements of pre-2024 results (Trevisan-Weber 2001, Helou-Terjanian 2008, Hussein 2018, McIntosh's computational verification to 10^9/10^11). The live Wikipedia article on Wolstenholme's theorem (checked directly) still states the converse as an open conjecture, citing a 2022 Booker-Hathi-Mossinghoff-Trudgian search establishing any unknown Wolstenholme prime exceeds 10^11 — that search itself predates the frozen revision and, per §3.1's rule on existence/infinitude questions and record-extension, would not count as settling the converse even if it were newer, since it narrows where a counterexample could hide rather than answering the question. No AI system was found involved in any work on this specific converse conjecture.
competing_reading: The Yaqubi-Mirzavaziri papers could be read more generously: if their generalized binom(np-1,p) congruence framework happens to yield, as a special/limiting case, a new statement about which composite n satisfy the classical Wolstenholme congruence, that would count as partial progress. I could not access the full text of either paper (ResearchGate and the Isfahan journal site both blocked automated fetches with 403/connection errors) to rule this out definitively — I relied on abstract summaries via search snippets, which consistently describe the subject as the Guo-Krattenthaler np-1-choose-p conjectures, not the prime-vs-composite converse.
what_would_settle_it: Obtaining the full text of 'Extending Wolstenholme's Theorem: A New Perspective' and 'New results on Wolstenholme's theorem and its applications' (e.g. via the DOI 10.22108/msci.2025.141789.1669 or a non-blocked mirror) to check definitively whether any theorem in them restricts the set of composite n satisfying binom(2n-1,n-1) ≡ 1 (mod n^3).
